listening.title: Booking the Community Sports Hall
listening.focus: Everyday conversation: main ideas, details and a change to a booking
listening.script:
STAFF: Good morning, Riverside Community Centre, Anna speaking. How can I help?
DANIEL: Hi, I'd like to book the small sports hall for a birthday party next month.
STAFF: Of course. Which date are you thinking about?
DANIEL: Saturday, the 14th of November, in the afternoon.
STAFF: Let me check... Yes, the small hall is free on Saturday the 14th. We have a large hall too, but the small one is good for up to 30 people.
DANIEL: That's perfect. There will be about 20 children and a few parents.
STAFF: How long do you need it for?
DANIEL: Maybe from 2 to 5? Actually, sorry, from 2 to 4 - two hours is enough.
STAFF: So 2pm to 4pm on Saturday the 14th of November. Noted. The cost is £25 per hour, so £50 in total.
DANIEL: That's fine. Do we need to pay now?
STAFF: You pay a £20 deposit today to keep the booking, and the rest on the day.
DANIEL: Okay. Can we bring our own food and music?
STAFF: Yes, you can bring cold food and your own speaker for music. But please note, sports shoes must be worn in the hall - no outdoor shoes.
DANIEL: I understand. Do you provide tables and chairs?
STAFF: Yes, we put out six tables and 25 chairs for free. If you need more, just tell us before Thursday the 12th.
DANIEL: Six tables is enough. Where do we collect the key?
STAFF: Come to the main desk on the ground floor 15 minutes early, and bring your booking email as proof.
DANIEL: Great. And is there parking?
STAFF: Yes, there is free parking behind the centre for about 40 cars.
STAFF: One last thing - please leave the hall tidy and put rubbish in the bins outside.
DANIEL: Of course, we'll clean up after the party.
STAFF: Thanks. I'll send the booking email with the deposit link today.
DANIEL: Thanks for your help, Anna. See you on the 14th.

reading.title: A Student Kitchen Rota That Works
reading.focus: Finding main ideas, details and the difference between a claim and an example
reading.passage:
Living with five other first-year students was new for Josh. At first, everyone enjoyed the freedom, but the shared kitchen quickly became a problem. Dirty plates covered the table, the floor was sticky, and nobody took out the rubbish. After two weeks, the group met and agreed to try a weekly kitchen rota.
The rota is simple and is fixed to the fridge door. Each student has one main job for a week, and the jobs change every Monday. The five jobs are: washing dishes, cleaning the cooker, cleaning the floor, taking out rubbish and recycling, and cleaning the fridge and shelves. Because there are six students and only five jobs, one person each week is free from kitchen work. This free week keeps the system fair and gives everyone a short break.
The author believes the rota works mainly because the rules are short and clear, not because students are punished. For example, Mia once forgot to clean the fridge during her week, and instead of paying money, she simply swapped weeks with Tom. The group thinks talking and swapping is better than strict fines.
Each job has three clear steps. For instance, 'cleaning the floor' means first moving the bins, then sweeping, then washing with hot water. A box under the sink holds sponges, soap and bags, so no one can say they cannot find the tools. The group also keeps a shared list on the fridge for cleaning products. When soap or bags run out, anyone writes the item on the list. On Monday, the student who is free from kitchen jobs buys these items, and everyone pays an equal share. This small rule stops arguments about money.
Every Sunday evening, the group spends ten minutes checking the kitchen together. If a job is not finished, the same person completes it that evening. There have been small problems. During exam weeks, some students are too busy to do their job well. To solve this, the group allows a busy student to ask another person to help, but the busy student must do that person's shopping in return. This exchange keeps the work balanced.
After two months, the kitchen is much cleaner. Josh says the best result is not just a clean room. Students now cook together more often and share food. The rota did not remove all arguments, but it gave the flat a fair way to discuss problems.

exercises.title: A Student Kitchen Rota That Works
exercises.focus: Finding main ideas, details and the difference between a claim and an example
exercises.passage:
Living with five other first-year students was new for Josh. At first, everyone enjoyed the freedom, but the shared kitchen quickly became a problem. Dirty plates covered the table, the floor was sticky, and nobody took out the rubbish. After two weeks, the group met and agreed to try a weekly kitchen rota.
The rota is simple and is fixed to the fridge door. Each student has one main job for a week, and the jobs change every Monday. The five jobs are: washing dishes, cleaning the cooker, cleaning the floor, taking out rubbish and recycling, and cleaning the fridge and shelves. Because there are six students and only five jobs, one person each week is free from kitchen work. This free week keeps the system fair and gives everyone a short break.
The author believes the rota works mainly because the rules are short and clear, not because students are punished. For example, Mia once forgot to clean the fridge during her week, and instead of paying money, she simply swapped weeks with Tom. The group thinks talking and swapping is better than strict fines.
Each job has three clear steps. For instance, 'cleaning the floor' means first moving the bins, then sweeping, then washing with hot water. A box under the sink holds sponges, soap and bags, so no one can say they cannot find the tools. The group also keeps a shared list on the fridge for cleaning products. When soap or bags run out, anyone writes the item on the list. On Monday, the student who is free from kitchen jobs buys these items, and everyone pays an equal share. This small rule stops arguments about money.
Every Sunday evening, the group spends ten minutes checking the kitchen together. If a job is not finished, the same person completes it that evening. There have been small problems. During exam weeks, some students are too busy to do their job well. To solve this, the group allows a busy student to ask another person to help, but the busy student must do that person's shopping in return. This exchange keeps the work balanced.
After two months, the kitchen is much cleaner. Josh says the best result is not just a clean room. Students now cook together more often and share food. The rota did not remove all arguments, but it gave the flat a fair way to discuss problems.
exercises.prompt: What was the problem at the start?
options: Students did not like cooking together
The shared kitchen was dirty and messy
There were no cleaning tools in the flat
Students argued about shopping money
exercises.explanation: The opening describes dirty plates, a sticky floor and rubbish not taken out. The cooking-together option fails because that is a later positive result.

writingPrompts.focus: Describing a table with clear comparisons
writingPrompts.prompt: The table below shows how many students signed up for five volunteer jobs at Greenfield College on Volunteer Sign-up Day on 12 March. Job type: Library help - 18 students; Park cleaning - 34 students; Food bank packing - 26 students; Animal shelter help - 14 students; Reading help for young children - 22 students. All sign-ups were for Saturday morning work in April. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words in about 20 minutes.

writingPrompts.focus: Summarising borrowing numbers and simple changes
writingPrompts.prompt: The table below shows how many times students at Riverside School borrowed four types of sports equipment from the school sports room in March and April. Footballs: March 42 times, April 55 times; Basketballs: March 38 times, April 36 times; Tennis rackets: March 20 times, April 28 times; Badminton sets: March 25 times, April 24 times. Students can borrow equipment for free for two days. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words in about 20 minutes.

writingPrompts.focus: Giving a clear opinion with direct reasons
writingPrompts.prompt: Some teachers think every secondary school student should do two hours of volunteer work each month, for example cleaning a park or helping in a library. Others think students are already busy with study and should not have to volunteer. Do you agree or disagree that schools should ask all students to do regular volunteer work? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own experience. Write at least 250 words in about 40 minutes.

Many schools let students borrow sports equipment such as balls and rackets for free. Some people say this is good because more students will play sport and stay healthy. Others say free borrowing causes problems because equipment gets lost or damaged. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own experience. Write at least 250 words in about 40 minutes.

writingPrompts.task: Task 2 · Planning a Small Class Picnic
writingPrompts.focus: Comparing choices and explaining a preference
writingPrompts.prompt: A class of 30 students wants to plan a small end-of-term picnic in a local park. Some students want the whole class to plan everything together, including food, transport and games. Others think it is faster and easier if the teacher makes all the decisions. Which way of planning do you think is better? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own experience. Write at least 250 words in about 40 minutes.

speakingPrompts.prompt: Answer these short questions about helping others. Give 2-3 sentences for each answer. 1. Did you ever help as a volunteer at school? 2. What kind of volunteer work do students in your area often do? 3. Do you prefer helping alone or helping with friends? Why? 4. Do you think you will do more volunteer work next year? Why or why not?

Answer these short questions about sport and free time. Give 2-3 sentences for each answer. 1. What sports do you often play or watch? 2. Do you ever borrow sports equipment from school or friends? 3. Where do people in your area usually play sport? 4. Do you prefer playing sport indoors or outdoors? Why?

speakingPrompts.task: Part 2 · Cue card · A Volunteer Day You Joined
speakingPrompts.focus: Describing a past event with clear sequence
speakingPrompts.prompt: Talk about a volunteer sign-up day or volunteer activity you joined or saw at school. You have one minute to prepare and should speak for one to two minutes. You should say: • what the activity was • when and where it happened • who joined with you • and explain why you remember it well or what you learned from it.

speakingPrompts.task: Part 2 · Cue card · Planning a Small Picnic
speakingPrompts.focus: Explaining a simple plan and personal role
speakingPrompts.prompt: Talk about a time when you helped plan a small picnic or class trip. You have one minute to prepare and should speak for one to two minutes. You should say: • where you wanted to go • who planned it with you • what food, transport or games you prepared • and explain if the plan worked well and why.

speakingPrompts.task: Part 3 · School Events and Community Help
speakingPrompts.prompt: Answer these questions as you would with an examiner. Give reasons and examples, not just short answers. 1. Why do some students join volunteer activities while others do not? 2. What are the advantages for a school when it organises a volunteer sign-up day? 3. How can schools make borrowing sports equipment fair for all students? 4. When a class plans a picnic together, what problems can happen and how can they solve them?
